name: Lorient
title: Lorient UTM and Hull Gauging | Fishing, Naval & Cargo Ships
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement at Lorient: trawlers at Keroman, cargo ships at Kergroise, repair-yard craft, hull, tank and piping UTM.
h1: Ship Thickness Gauging in Lorient and the Rade
intro: Lorient is Brittany's great fishing port and a naval shipbuilding town, with a commercial harbour for fertiliser, fodder and petroleum cargoes on the same sheltered rade. Fishing vessels, naval craft, repair-yard visitors and short-sea cargo ships all need their steel measured at some point. Atlantis sends technicians from India to the quay for each job, with the work shaped by the landing schedule and the tide.

highlights.h: A large fishing fleet to measure
highlights.p: Keroman is a major fishing port, with trawlers and deep-sea vessels that land, refuel and wait on the quay. Hull, fish hold and tank readings are fitted around landings and the sailing day.
Ship repair is part of the port's identity. A vessel in for repair can have its steel measured early in the stay, so the work list reflects what the structure actually needs.
Fertiliser, fodder and petroleum cargoes arrive on coasters and small tankers. Their longer stays at the commercial quay suit hold, coaming and ballast tank gauging.

port.h: Lorient: a fishing harbour on a sheltered rade
p: Lorient lies on the southern coast of Brittany where the rivers Scorff and Blavet flow into a broad, sheltered roadstead, the Rade de Lorient, closed at its mouth by Port-Louis and the citadel. The harbour is divided by function. Keroman, on the western shore, is the fishing port, with a large fish market, cold stores and a fleet of trawlers and deep-sea vessels. The commercial port at Kergroise handles dry and liquid bulk. A naval shipyard, long established on the site, builds and maintains warships, and the old submarine pens of the Keroman base stand as a landmark. Ferries run from the harbour to the island of Groix.

The ships that are measured here are therefore a varied group. Fishing vessels are the most numerous, from coastal boats to large trawlers and vessels for longer voyages, and they return to Keroman to land, refuel and rest. Short-sea cargo ships call at Kergroise with fertiliser, animal fodder, wood and petroleum products for Brittany's farms and industry. Naval auxiliaries and civil support ships work from the shipyard side, and the port has become a base for the supply chain of offshore renewable energy, which brings project cargo and service vessels onto the quays.

Lorient is exposed to Atlantic weather but protected by the rade, so launch work is possible on most days and berths are mostly sheltered. The port's tide is moderate compared with the Channel ports. Ship repair here is on a small and medium scale: yards in and around the rade work on fishing vessels, tugs, patrol craft and coastal ships, and larger ships needing a major docking usually go to Brest, Saint-Nazaire or a yard abroad. Thickness gauging at Lorient therefore falls into two groups: routine condition measurement of working fleets, and steel assessment for ships that are in repair or about to move on for a docking.

facilities.h: Where ships can be gauged at Lorient
p: At Keroman the fishing quays give access to vessels between trips. A trawler lies alongside for a day or two while it lands its catch, takes ice and fuel and changes crew, and during that time the hull above the waterline, deck plating, fish holds, fuel and ballast tanks and accessible piping can be measured. Fish holds need to be cleaned and ventilated, and the crew prepare them in advance. Fishing vessels are frequently older steel hulls with a long record of repair, so the readings help the owner choose between further repair and replacement.

At Kergroise a coaster or small tanker is gauged at the commercial quay, with holds, hatch covers and tanks measured when empty. The repair yards of the rade offer a different kind of access: ships in for repair afloat or on a yard's facilities are open to the superintendent, and early readings let the repair list be drawn up before the steel work starts. Ships at anchor in the rade are reached by launch, and the shelter of the roadstead keeps that practical in most conditions. The naval shipyard is a restricted area, and gauging there is outside what we do.
list: Keroman fishing quays — hull, fish hold, fuel tank and piping gauging on trawlers and deep-sea fishing vessels between trips.
Kergroise commercial quays — hold, coaming, hatch cover and ballast tank gauging on short-sea cargo ships and small tankers.
Repair yard berths on the rade — early steel assessment on fishing vessels, tugs and coastal ships in for repair.
Rade de Lorient anchorage — launch-served readings on ships waiting for a berth or a yard slot.
Groix ferry berth — deck, ramp and tank checks on small ro-pax craft during layovers.
Offshore energy support quays — hull and deck gauging on service and supply vessels between operations.

p: Port state control in France follows the Paris MoU, and the Centres de sécurité des navires of the French maritime administration also oversee the safety of French-flag fishing vessels and coastal ships. Visible wastage on a fishing vessel's hull or a tank leak is the kind of finding that can hold a boat in port, so owners often have the steel measured before their annual safety inspection. For foreign-flag cargo ships at Kergroise, the same risk-based targeting applies as in any other Paris MoU port.

Fishing vessels follow national safety rules rather than the classification regime used by large merchant ships, though many are classed voluntarily, and thickness readings support both. Short-sea cargo ships and small tankers follow their class society's survey rules, with the Enhanced Survey Programme applying to tankers and bulk carriers. EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime affect larger ships on EU voyages, and the EU Ship Recycling Regulation's Inventory of Hazardous Materials applies to ships over 500 gross tonnage calling at EU ports. For owners deciding on renewal or replacement of an older hull, measured steel is the basis of the decision.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs in Lorient
jobs.p: Requests from Lorient come from fishing fleet owners, cargo ship managers and repair yards. The common thread is steel assessment: how much has been lost, where, and whether a repair or a docking can wait. We work from the owner's list of concerns and the class or flag requirements, and agree with the superintendent which spaces are accessible during the stay at the quay. Typical jobs include:
list: Hull plating, fish hold and fuel tank gauging on a trawler during a landing and refuelling stop at Keroman.
Pre-repair steel assessment on a fishing vessel that has just entered a yard in the rade, so the work list matches the measured wastage.
Hold, coaming and hatch cover gauging on a coaster discharging fertiliser or fodder at Kergroise.
Ballast tank and deck gauging on a small tanker waiting at the commercial quay between cargoes.
Condition gauging for a buyer of a second-hand fishing vessel or coastal ship lying alongside in the harbour.

logistics: The regional airport at Lorient offers connections to Paris, and from India the usual route is an international flight to Paris Charles de Gaulle followed by a domestic flight or a TGV train to Lorient. The ship's agent or the owner arranges access to Keroman, Kergroise or the repair yards, and books a launch for ships in the rade. The naval areas are closed to civilians. France is in the Schengen area, so each technician needs a Schengen visa, which we apply for once the stay is confirmed, with an invitation letter from the owner naming the ship.

faqs.q: Can a trawler be gauged during a landing stop at Keroman?
faqs.a: Yes. A trawler is alongside for a day or two, and the hull, deck plating, fuel tanks and cleaned fish holds can be measured during that time. The crew prepare the holds and tanks in advance, and we plan the sequence around landing and refuelling so that the work does not interfere with the vessel's turnaround.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock at Lorient for a docking survey?
faqs.a: Yards in and around the rade handle repair and docking for fishing vessels, tugs and coastal ships. Larger ships needing a major docking usually go to Brest, Saint-Nazaire or a yard abroad. We gauge at Lorient beforehand where needed, so the repair list reflects measured steel.

faqs.q: Can you work on naval vessels at Lorient?
faqs.a: The naval shipyard and naval berths are restricted areas, and we do not work there. Our work in Lorient is for owners and managers of merchant and fishing vessels, at the commercial and fishing quays, the repair berths and the roadstead anchorage.

faqs.q: What can be combined with thickness gauging on a fishing vessel?
faqs.a: Magnetic particle or dye penetrant checks on winch foundations, gantry and net-drum supports, and ultrasonic checks of weld repairs, are often combined with hull thickness readings. Piping wall-thickness checks on fuel, bilge and sea-water systems fit the same visit, because the permits and access are already in place.
